name: Geetha
definition: Geetha is a composite portrait of a powerloom weaver and homemaker in Honnali town, Davanagere district, navigating the decline of the region's handloom tradition while raising two school-age children and managing household expenses on fluctuating piece-rate income. She draws on the experiences of Padmashali weavers in Honnali and surrounding taluks who have shifted from traditional handlooms to powerlooms or migrated to Davanagere city's textile units, balancing pride in their craft heritage with the economic pressures of competition from Surat and Ichalkaranji synthetic fabrics.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Geetha works from home on a rented powerloom, weaving cotton and blended-fabric sarees and dhotis on order from a Honnali-based master weaver who supplies yarn and collects finished pieces twice a week. She earns between ₹6,000 and ₹9,000 a month depending on orders, down from steadier income a decade ago when Davanagere's mill-town legacy still supported local weaving. The loom occupies one room of their small rented house; she begins work at six in the morning after sending her children to school, breaks for cooking and household tasks, and resumes in the afternoon until seven or eight in the evening. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on the Honnali-Davanagere route, bringing in another ₹8,000-10,000 monthly, but diesel costs and vehicle repairs eat into earnings. Power cuts are less frequent now but still disrupt her weaving schedule. The master weaver's orders have shrunk as cheap synthetic sarees flood the market; Geetha worries the next lean season will force her to look for daily-wage work in Davanagere's garment units or as a domestic helper, leaving the loom idle.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Geetha lives with her husband and their two children: a daughter in Class 8 and a son in Class 5, both studying at the Honnali government Kannada-medium high school. Her husband's mother, widowed five years ago, lives in their ancestral village near Channagiri and visits during festival seasons; Geetha sends her ₹1,000-1,500 monthly for medicines. Geetha married at nineteen, shortly after completing her PUC, in an arranged match within the Padmashali community; her parents, small farmers near Jagalur, could not afford further education. Her daily routine revolves around the children's school timings, cooking two full meals, managing the loom and keeping the household accounts. Her daughter helps with cooking and younger-sibling care after school; Geetha insists she focus on studies and not learn weaving unless she chooses it after finishing school. Her husband's income is unpredictable, so Geetha controls most spending decisions, saving small amounts in a local chit fund when orders are good. Gender roles are traditional but negotiated: her husband expects meals on time, yet he also fetches vegetables from the market and helps the children with homework when she is at the loom late.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Geetha completed her PUC at a government college in Jagalur taluk but could not pursue a degree; her parents needed her earnings and arranged her marriage soon after. She is determined that both her children finish at least degree-level education. Her daughter, now in Class 8, is a steady student who wants to become a teacher; Geetha dreams of enrolling her in a private PU college in Davanagere if they can afford it, hoping the English-medium environment will open government-job or private-sector opportunities the Kannada-medium track rarely provides. Her son is less academically inclined but enjoys drawing; she has enrolled him in a weekend art class run by a local NGO at minimal cost. School fees are low—textbooks, uniforms and the midday meal are free—but extras add up: notebooks, pens, school-trip contributions, tuition for mathematics and science (₹500 per child per month), and the daughter's recently purchased mobile phone for online lessons during the pandemic, now used for schoolwork and entertainment. Geetha worries the daughter will face marriage pressure from relatives once she crosses sixteen, and she argues with her husband and mother-in-law to let the girl study further, pointing to friends' daughters who now hold bank or anganwadi jobs after degrees.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Geetha and her family rely on the Honnali government taluk hospital for routine care and the Ayushman Bharat card for major expenses; her mother-in-law's cataract surgery last year cost nothing out-of-pocket under the scheme, though the family had to pay for transport and attendant meals in Davanagere. Geetha suffers from chronic lower-back pain, which she attributes to long hours at the loom, and occasional wrist soreness; she takes over-the-counter painkillers from the local pharmacy and has never consulted a specialist. Her children are generally healthy, though her son had a prolonged fever two years ago that required a week's private-clinic treatment and antibiotics costing ₹3,000, draining their savings. Honnali's water supply comes from borewells and the Bhadra canal when it flows; Geetha boils drinking water during the monsoon, fearing contamination. She has heard of fluorosis in neighbouring Kolar and Chikkaballapur but believes Davanagere's water is safer. The anganwadi where she once took her children for growth monitoring has closed its local outpost; the nearest functional one is a kilometre away. Geetha worries about her daughter's iron levels—she looks pale and tires easily—but cannot afford regular doctor visits or the iron supplements the ASHA worker recommended.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Geetha belongs to the Padmashali weaver community, traditionally associated with handloom craft and historically classified under OBC. Her family observes festivals like Ugadi, Deepavali and Varamahalakshmi Vrata, and they visit the Honnali Anjaneya temple and the nearby Eshwara temple during Shivaratri. Her husband's family has loose ties to a local Veerashaiva-Lingayat mutt, though they are not initiated devotees; they attend the mutt's annual jathra and occasionally receive prasada and educational support from its outreach programmes. Geetha's social circle consists of a few neighbouring women—some weavers, others farmers' wives or anganwadi helpers—with whom she shares chit-fund membership, childcare advice and festival preparations. Caste remains a quiet but present force: Padmashali families prefer endogamous marriages, and Geetha's husband once mentioned that their daughter should marry within the community, though Geetha privately hopes education will give her daughter more choice. She feels proud of her weaving heritage but frustrated that the market no longer values it; she tells her children the Padmashali past was noble, but survival today requires degrees and salaries, not looms.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Geetha has an Ayushman Bharat card and a ration card; the family receives five kilograms of subsidised rice and two of wheat monthly, which helps but does not cover their needs. She enrolled for a loan under the Stree Shakti scheme three years ago to buy the powerloom but struggled with the paperwork and ultimately borrowed from a chit fund instead. Her husband uses the Shakti bus-pass benefit to travel to Davanagere for auto-rickshaw association meetings, which saves their household ₹100-150 weekly. Geetha has never attended a gram panchayat or town municipal council meeting but knows the local Congress councillor by face; her husband once approached him to fix a pothole on their street, which took six months. She blames both the state and central governments for failing to protect handloom weavers from synthetic-fabric dumping, though she is unclear on what policy could help. She believes government schools are improving—her children's teachers are more regular now than when she was a student—but worries that without private tuition, her children will fall behind in competitive exams.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Geetha is proud of her ability to weave sarees her grandmother would recognise and to juggle loom work, household tasks and children's schooling on a tight budget; she sees herself as carrying forward a centuries-old Padmashali craft tradition even as the market marginalises it. She worries most about the next lean season when weaving orders dry up, the daughter's future—whether they can afford PU college in Davanagere or whether relatives' marriage talk will derail her studies—and her son's weaker academic performance. She blames Surat and Ichalkaranji synthetic-saree manufacturers for killing local weaving, but also the master weavers who squeeze piece-rates, and the government for failing to enforce handloom protections or create steady work. She demands better schools in Honnali so families do not have to send children to Davanagere, more healthcare staff at the taluk hospital so she does not lose half a day waiting, and a support price or guaranteed orders for handloom weavers as farmers have for crops. She is sceptical that any government—Congress, BJP or JD(S)—will deliver, but the Gruha Lakshmi cash has made her feel, for the first time, that someone in power acknowledged women's unpaid work. She resents that Honnali and Davanagere's mill-town past brought prosperity to owners and traders but left weavers like her scrambling, and she is determined her children will escape the loom through education, even if that means the craft dies with her generation.
